title: Type I and Type II Errors
body:
A [[Hypothesis Testing|test]] produces a verdict, the world has a truth, and they need not match.
There are exactly two ways to be wrong and they are not symmetric.

|  | $H_0$ is true | $H_0$ is false |
|---|---|---|
| **Reject $H_0$** | **Type I error**, probability $\alpha$ | correct, probability $1-\beta$ (**power**) |
| **Fail to reject** | correct, probability $1-\alpha$ | **Type II error**, probability $\beta$ |

- **Type I: rejecting a true null.** You claim an effect that is not there. A **false positive**.
  Its rate is $\alpha$, and $\alpha$ is not estimated from data, it is *chosen* before the study.
- **Type II: failing to reject a false null.** You miss a real effect. A **false negative**. Its
  rate is $\beta$, and unlike $\alpha$ it depends on how big the true effect is, so it is not a
  single number until you name an effect size to detect.

**Power is $1 - \beta$**, the probability of catching a real effect of a given size. It is what a
sample-size calculation solves for.

Mnemonic that survives exams: Type I is crying wolf when there is none, Type II is missing the wolf
that is there.

## The trade-off, and the only way out

$\alpha$ and $\beta$ move in opposite directions **for a fixed $n$**. Demanding stronger evidence
before rejecting (smaller $\alpha$) means rejecting less often, including when you should, which
raises $\beta$. Every threshold choice is a position on that curve, not an escape from it.

The one thing that improves both at once is **more data**, because a smaller standard error
separates the two sampling distributions and shrinks the overlap they share. That is the whole
argument for statistical power calculations.

The four levers on power:

| Lever | Effect on power |
|---|---|
| larger $n$ | up, at rate $\sqrt{n}$ |
| larger true effect | up (nothing you control) |
| smaller $\sigma$ | up (better measurement, paired design) |
| larger $\alpha$ | up, by trading Type I risk for it |

**Which error is worse is a domain question, not a statistical one.** A screening test wants a tiny
$\beta$ and tolerates false alarms, because a missed cancer costs more than an unnecessary follow-up.
A criminal trial sets $H_0$ to "innocent" and drives $\alpha$ very low, accepting that guilty people
go free. A spam filter would rather deliver junk than eat a real message. Statistics gives you the
dial; the cost of each mistake decides where to set it.

## The same table in fourth-year computer science

This is the note the machine learning evaluation vocabulary hangs from. A classifier's
[[Confusion Matrix]] is **this table with the labels changed**: predictions instead of test verdicts,
ground truth instead of $H_0$.

| Statistics | Classification | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| Type I error, rate $\alpha$ | [[False Positive]] | predicted positive, actually negative |
| Type II error, rate $\beta$ | [[False Negative]] | predicted negative, actually positive |
| correct rejection of a false $H_0$ | [[True Positive]] | predicted positive, actually positive |
| correct non-rejection | [[True Negative]] | predicted negative, actually negative |
| power, $1-\beta$ | [[Sensitivity]] (recall, true positive rate) | $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})$ |
| $1-\alpha$ | [[Specificity]] (true negative rate) | $\text{TN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FP})$ |

**And a $2 \times 2$ contingency table is the same object again**, which is the neat part: the
[[Chi-Square Test]] tests exactly this grid for independence, while a classifier summarises it into
rates. One four-cell table, three vocabularies.

Two things transfer directly with the vocabulary:

- **The trade-off does not go away.** Moving a classifier's decision threshold slides you along the
  same curve, buying [[Sensitivity]] with [[Specificity]]. An ROC curve is a plot of that curve, and
  it is $\alpha$ against $1-\beta$ drawn for every threshold at once.
- **Precision is not power, and it depends on the base rate.** $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})$ can
  be terrible even with excellent sensitivity when positives are rare, which is the medical-test
  arithmetic in [[Bayes Theorem]] arriving from the other direction. This is why accuracy is a
  useless metric on imbalanced data, and why [[Stratification]] matters when splitting it.

## Related

- [[Hypothesis Testing]]: the procedure these are the failure modes of
- [[P-VALUES]]: $p < \alpha$ is where the Type I risk is spent
- [[Bayes Theorem]]: base rates, and why a positive result on a rare condition is usually wrong
- [[Confusion Matrix]], [[Classification]], [[MACHINE LEARNING]]: the same table, applied
- [[Chi-Square Test]]: the contingency-table view of it
- [[Sensitivity]] and [[Specificity]]: power and $1-\alpha$ under their
  classification names, with the precision-versus-recall distinction spelled out
- [[Stratification]]: the sampling method that keeps a train/test split from skewing these rates
